meaning: The external form of the problem of evil asserts an evil premise as true. In its moral-evil version the premise is that there is man-made evil, murder and rape, which are evil. From O'Connor's emotivism (moral statements have no truth value), his own gloss (what has no truth value is not true), his classification of badness ascriptions as moral, and his own treatment of man-made evil as moral wrongness (2016), it follows that this premise is not true. The external form therefore contradicts his commitments. Each bridge is its own sourced statement. The theorem denies truth (Holds); it reaches 'objectively true' only under the further, unformalized bridge that what is objectively true is true. Scope: the natural-evil version (earthquakes) is not covered. O'Connor says we call those evil because they harm us, a different claim, and such a version needs an evaluative premise of its own (for instance 'a loving god would not permit such suffering', OCONNOR-CHRISTIANITYS-BIGGEST-PROBLEM-SUFFERING), to which the same three steps would apply once that premise is classified as moral. The internal form is answered separately (POE-CATHOLIC-CONSISTENT-WITH-EVIL). Proof shape, stated plainly: three steps (the premise is moral because it says something is bad; emotivism then denies it a truth value; the gloss then denies it truth). No premise already states the conclusion.
